title: A Method for Generating Semantically Opaque Interface Identifiers with IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC)
summary: Describes how a host can build the host-specific half of its IPv6 address so that it stays the same within one network but changes when the host moves to another network. This is an alternative to deriving the address from the hardware (MAC) address, which would let people track a device everywhere. It keeps the benefits of stable addresses without the privacy cost.

eli5.summary: Imagine you get a new nickname at every school you attend. Within one school the nickname never changes, so friends can find you, but nobody can follow you from school to school.

questions: how to generate ipv6 interface identifiers
how to generate stable ipv6 interface identifiers
how does ipv6 avoid tracking by mac address
subtitle: A hash-based recipe for IPv6 addresses that stay put on one network but change when a host moves to another.

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses built from a hardware address never change, so they let others track a device across networks, hint at its vendor, and help attackers scan for hosts.
tldr.mechanism: The host feeds the network prefix, an interface identifier, an optional network ID, a duplicate-address counter and a secret key into a pseudorandom function, and takes the low bits of the result as the Interface Identifier.
tldr.outcome: The address is stable within one subnet but differs from network to network. It is an alternative to hardware-based identifiers and does not replace temporary addresses.

today: RFC 7217 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is described as an alternative to hardware-based identifiers, not a deprecation of them.

sections.title: The Problem with Hardware-Based Identifiers
sections.content:
With IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862), a host usually builds a stable address from a network prefix advertised by a router plus an Interface Identifier (IID) that typically embeds a hardware (MAC) address. The RFC lists the drawbacks:

  • The IID never changes, so activity on one network can be correlated.
  • The IID is the same on every network, so a host can be tracked as it moves.
  • Address patterns, such as a vendor's OUI, shrink the search space for address-scanning attacks.
  • The hardware address leaks device-specific information.
  • Replacing the network card changes the address.

Privacy extensions (RFC 4941, temporary addresses) help only partly. They do not remove fixed identifiers used for server-like functions, and some organizations disable them because they complicate logging, troubleshooting and access control. So there is a motivation to improve the stable addresses themselves.
sections.eli5: If your name tag always shows the same serial number, anyone can recognize you wherever you go. This RFC gives you a name tag that changes at each place.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Standards
sections.content:
The method is orthogonal to temporary addresses. With temporary addresses it improves the stable addresses used alongside them, and for hosts that disable temporary addresses it mitigates host-tracking and address scanning. It is aimed at SLAAC but can also be used with DHCPv6 or manual configuration.

It is incrementally deployable, since it creates no interoperability issues with nodes that do not use it. It does not modify SLAAC itself, so normal address lifetimes from the Prefix Information Options and renumbering behavior still apply. It also does not formally obsolete or deprecate any existing method of generating Interface Identifiers.
sections.eli5: This does not replace the old rules or the rotating nicknames. It just offers a better kind of permanent nickname that works next to them.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The RFC sets these goals for the resulting Interface Identifiers:

  • They stay the same for a given interface and prefix within the same subnet.
  • They change when the prefix changes, so it is hard to tell that two addresses belong to the same host.
  • An outsider cannot predict them, even knowing other IIDs the host generated.
  • Depending on the implementation, they are independent of the hardware, so replacing a network card or adding links to a Link Aggregation Group does not change the address.
  • They apply to all stable addresses, including global, link-local and unique-local ones.
sections.eli5: The nickname should stay the same in one school, be different in every other school, and be impossible to guess.

sections.title: The Generation Algorithm
sections.content:
Conforming implementations MUST use this algorithm for all stable SLAAC addresses, in place of methods like those in RFC 2464, and MAY also generate temporary addresses. First compute a random but stable identifier: RID = F(Prefix, Net_Iface, Network_ID, DAD_Counter, secret_key). Then take as many bits from the RID as needed, starting from the least significant bit.

  • F() is a pseudorandom function that must not be computable without the secret key and must be hard to reverse. It SHOULD produce at least 64 bits. A cryptographic hash such as SHA-1 or SHA-256 could be used; MD5 is unacceptable.
  • Prefix is the SLAAC prefix from a Router Advertisement, or the link-local prefix.
  • Net_Iface is a stable identifier of the interface. It MUST be constant across reboots and other network events, and different for each interface in simultaneous use.
  • Network_ID is optional data identifying the subnet, for example the 802.11 SSID.
  • DAD_Counter starts at 0 and resolves address conflicts.
  • secret_key SHOULD be at least 128 bits, MUST be initialized to a pseudo-random number when the system is installed or the IPv6 stack first starts, and should not be used for anything else.

The result SHOULD be checked against reserved Interface Identifiers and those already in use on the interface; a bad value is handled like a duplicate address. All bits are treated as opaque, including the universal/local bit. Because keys and functions differ, addresses are not expected to be stable across different operating-system installations. Implementations SHOULD let an administrator enable or disable the algorithm.
sections.eli5: The computer stirs together the street name, which door it is, and a secret recipe, and the result is its house number on that street. Same street gives the same number; a new street gives a new number.

sections.title: Resolving Address Conflicts
sections.content:
If Duplicate Address Detection shows the tentative address is already taken, the host SHOULD increment DAD_Counter by 1 and generate a new Interface Identifier with the same algorithm. It SHOULD wait a random delay between 0 and IDGEN_DELAY seconds first, to avoid lockstep behavior between hosts. It SHOULD try at least IDGEN_RETRIES addresses, but MUST limit how many it tries.

Hosts MAY record the counter for each {Prefix, Net_Iface, Network_ID} tuple in non-volatile memory, so a conflict resolved once is resolved the same way next time. This is optional. If the conflict cannot be solved, address configuration fails, and hosts MUST NOT automatically fall back to other algorithms for generating Interface Identifiers.

The specified constants are IDGEN_RETRIES, which defaults to 3, and IDGEN_DELAY, which defaults to 1 second.
sections.eli5: If two kids pick the same nickname, one waits a moment and picks again with a small twist. After a few tries it stops rather than guessing forever.

sections.title: Choosing the Net_Iface Source
sections.content:
Appendix A lists possible sources for Net_Iface, each with trade-offs:

  • Interface Index: unique within the node, but it may change when interfaces are added, removed or initialized in a different order.
  • Interface Name: more stable. Generic names like eth0 survive card replacement, while vendor-dependent names change with a different vendor's card.
  • Link-layer address: a fallback when the other two are not stable enough, but the IPv6 addresses then change when the card is replaced.
  • Logical network service identity: a UUID or similar identifier kept by operating systems that have such a concept.

The main text adds that a client system may prefer identifiers tied to the card, while a server system may prefer ones tied to the slot or port.
sections.eli5: The computer needs a permanent label for each network plug. Some labels survive swapping parts and some do not, so you pick based on what you care about.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compared with hardware-based identifiers, the method prevents trivial host tracking, since the prefix or Network_ID usually changes between networks. It also mitigates address scanning that relies on predictable IIDs, stops leakage of hardware addresses, and means one leaked IID does not harm the privacy of stable addresses for other prefixes.

One attack remains. An attacker on the same subnet can send a forged Router Advertisement for a prefix and learn the IID the victim would use for it. RA-Guard may stop the forged advertisement, and an unknown Network_ID would make the learned IID differ from the real one. If this attack becomes a concern, the host should consider SEND.

The privacy of the scheme depends on the secrecy of the key, so access to it should be restricted. The RFC states this is an alternative to hardware-based IIDs, not to temporary addresses, though it still benefits hosts that use temporary addresses.
sections.eli5: The secret recipe has to stay secret. If a troublemaker can trick your computer into revealing a nickname for one street, careful design keeps that from revealing your nicknames on other streets.

data.title: Random but stable identifier
data.code: RID = F(Prefix, Net_Iface, Network_ID, DAD_Counter, secret_key)

items.title: Prefix
items.text: Makes the identifier differ per prefix, and so per network.

items.title: Net_Iface
items.text: Stable identifier of the interface; must differ per interface.

items.title: Network_ID
items.text: Optional subnet data such as an SSID.

items.title: DAD_Counter
items.text: Starts at 0; incremented to resolve conflicts.
